1	# Osprey, Edited MRS, and Quantitative Reporting: Offline Research Dossier
2	
3	## Scope
4	
5	This packet provides broad scientific context for interpreting a historical
6	Osprey analysis. It is not a troubleshooting note. The bundled source and
7	complete upstream manuals define the exact data structures and implementation
8	available in this offline task.
9	
10	The material covers acquisition records, edited spectroscopy, spectral
11	combinations, basis modelling, macromolecular signals, processing, fitting,
12	reference data, relaxation, quantitative reporting, quality control, and
13	reproducibility.
14	
15	## Primary Osprey publication
16	
17	Georg Oeltzschner, Helge J. Zollner, Steve C. N. Hui, Mark Mikkelsen,
18	Muhammad G. Saleh, Sofie Tapper, and Richard A. E. Edden, "Osprey:
19	Open-source processing, reconstruction & estimation of magnetic resonance
20	spectroscopy data," *Journal of Neuroscience Methods* 343, 108827 (2020).
21	
22	- DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jneumeth.2020.108827
23	- PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32603810/
24	- PubMed Central record:
25	  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7477913/
26	
27	Osprey is an integrated workflow for loading, processing, modelling,
28	quantifying, visualizing, and exporting in-vivo magnetic resonance
29	spectroscopy data. The task source is an older project revision; current
30	online behavior must not be substituted for the bundled implementation.
31	
32	## Project workflow and container
33	
34	Osprey modules exchange information through an `MRSCont` container. A job
35	record selects files, sequence type, modelling options, references, anatomical
36	data, and outputs. Later modules add processed spectra, fitted model
37	parameters, basis representations, quality measures, quantitative values, and
38	reports.
39	
40	The major layers include:
41	
42	1. job construction and option validation;
43	2. vendor-file loading and conversion to common spectral structures;
44	3. coil combination, averaging, alignment, referencing, and other processing;
45	4. basis preparation and spectral fitting;
46	5. optional spatial registration and tissue segmentation;
47	6. calculation of several quantitative output families;
48	7. quality-control, overview, and export.
49	
50	The textual upstream manuals are available under:
51	
52	- `source/docs/`
53	- `source/docs_source/`
54	
55	These manuals and examples are part of the historical project source, not
56	task-specific answer material.
57	
58	## Spectroscopy data and metadata
59	
60	An MRS analysis may contain water-suppressed metabolite data, unsuppressed
61	reference data, short-echo water data, metabolite-nulled macromolecule data,
62	anatomical images, basis sets, and fitted checkpoints.
63	
64	Common metadata include field strength, nucleus, repetition time, echo time,
65	spectral width, dwell time, transmitter frequency, voxel geometry, sequence,
66	editing targets, and averaging information. Values can originate in scanner
67	headers, converted files, job options, or processed structures. Their meaning
68	must be established from the local source version and data contract.
69	
70	## Time and frequency representations
71	
72	An idealized time-domain signal is a sum of damped complex components. Fourier
73	transformation produces a spectrum whose peaks reflect resonance frequency,
74	phase, linewidth, and amplitude. Real data also contain residual water,
75	baseline structure, scanner drift, coil sensitivity, macromolecules, lipids,
76	noise, and imperfect localization.
77	
78	Processing can therefore affect the amplitude and phase conventions later
79	used by a fit. A numerically valid array is not sufficient evidence that two
80	arrays represent the same physical or algebraic spectrum.
81	
82	## Difference-edited spectroscopy
83	
84	MEGA editing acquires spectra under different editing-pulse conditions and
85	combines them to emphasize selected coupled resonances. HERMES and HERCULES use
86	Hadamard encoding to resolve multiple edited targets from a larger set of
87	acquisition states.
88	
89	Reference:
90	
91	Saleh M. G. et al., "HERMES: Hadamard encoding and reconstruction of
92	MEGA-edited spectroscopy," *Magnetic Resonance in Medicine*.
93	DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/mrm.26233
94	
95	Edited workflows can expose several algebraic spectra, such as individual
96	states, edit-OFF or edit-ON spectra, difference spectra, and sum spectra. The
97	number and order of these representations differ between MEGA, HERMES, and
98	HERCULES. Osprey basis sets store corresponding model spectra along a
99	sub-spectrum dimension.
100	
101	A sum, difference, or Hadamard-reconstructed spectrum is not automatically on
102	the same amplitude convention as one contributing acquisition state. Data and
103	basis functions must use compatible conventions when a model is transferred
104	between representations.
105	
106	## Basis sets and linear-combination modelling
107	
108	Osprey represents a measured spectrum as a combination of simulated or
109	measured basis functions plus baseline and lineshape terms. Basis sets can
110	contain metabolites, macromolecular components, and lipids. Their metadata
111	describe the sequence, field strength, echo time, spectral width, number of
112	points, and sub-spectrum layout.
113	
114	Important modelling choices include:
115	
116	- basis-set composition and naming;
117	- fit range and baseline flexibility;
118	- separate versus concatenated fitting;
119	- treatment of edited sub-spectra;
120	- shared or independent parameters across spectra;
121	- macromolecule and lipid models;
122	- sequence-specific basis selection;
123	- field-strength and echo-time compatibility.
124	
125	The bundled manual chapter `source/docs/the-osprey-job-file.html` documents
126	the available fitting styles and co-edited macromolecule options for this
127	project generation.
128	
129	## Co-edited macromolecular signals
130	
131	GABA-edited spectra contain a co-edited macromolecular contribution near
132	3 ppm. Osprey provides several modelling strategies, including fixed,
133	soft-constrained, and freely modelled forms. Some strategies relate the
134	3-ppm component to another macromolecular component or to a fitted metabolite
135	reference.
136	
137	The physical calibration involves peak areas, proton counts, linewidths, and
138	the spectral representation used in a fit. Reported model families differ in
139	which components are explicit, which are constrained, and which fitted
140	quantities are subsequently exported.
141	
142	The following method record supplies additional context:
143	
144	Zollner H. J. et al., "Comparison of linear combination modeling strategies
145	for GABA-edited MRS at 3T."
146	DOI: https://doi.org/10.1101/2021.05.26.445817
147	
148	## Processing and alignment
149	
150	Typical processing includes coil combination, averaging, frequency and phase
151	alignment, eddy-current correction, spectral referencing, residual-water
152	handling, and sub-spectrum combination. Edited acquisitions additionally
153	require correct ordering and polarity of acquisition states before algebraic
154	combination.
155	
156	Changes in processing can alter phase, linewidth, residual structure, or
157	amplitude. A model discrepancy may therefore originate before, during, or
158	after basis preparation.
159	
160	## Reference strategies and quantitative outputs
161	
162	MRS software can report fitted amplitudes, ratios to creatine, ratios to an
163	unsuppressed water signal, CSF-corrected values, tissue-corrected values, and
164	model-quality measures. These outputs are not interchangeable.
165	
166	Water-referenced estimates combine fitted metabolite and reference signals
167	with acquisition metadata and, depending on the reporting mode, relaxation or
168	tissue information. A separate short-echo water acquisition and a lineshape
169	reference can serve different scientific roles.
170	
171	## Relaxation and acquisition protocol
172	
173	Longitudinal recovery and transverse attenuation depend on acquisition timing
174	and relaxation constants. Metabolites, water, tissues, field strengths, and
175	sequences can use different literature values. Historical implementations may
176	contain lookup tables, fallback values, or branches for supported field
177	strengths.
178	
179	A quantitative correction must interpret stored acquisition metadata and
180	literature constants consistently. Implementations also need to preserve the
181	distinction between scanner metadata, processed-data metadata, fitted signal
182	parameters, and report-level quantities.
183	
184	## Tissue and CSF corrections
185	
186	If anatomical segmentation is available, a workflow may combine gray-matter,
187	white-matter, and CSF fractions with tissue water content and relaxation
188	behavior. Osprey also reports simpler output families that do not require
189	segmentation. Comparisons must identify which output family and correction
190	level are being used.
191	
192	Reference:
193	
194	Gasparovic C. et al., "Use of tissue water as a concentration reference for
195	proton spectroscopic imaging," *Magnetic Resonance in Medicine* 55(6),
196	1219-1226 (2006). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/mrm.20901
197	
198	## FID-A and shared scientific code
199	
200	Osprey includes code derived from the FID-A toolbox for spectral structures,
201	processing operations, simulation, and model support.
202	
203	Simpson R. et al., "Advanced processing and simulation of MRS data using the
204	FID appliance (FID-A)," *Magnetic Resonance in Medicine*.
205	DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/mrm.26091
206	
207	The local FID-A snapshot is included under `source/libraries/FID-A/` so that
208	the task can run and be inspected without network access.
209	
210	## Quality control and reproducibility
211	
212	Relevant quality indicators include signal-to-noise ratio, linewidth,
213	frequency and phase stability, residual water, fit residuals, baseline
214	behavior, and model uncertainty. Reproducible reporting should also identify
215	the acquisition protocol, basis set, preprocessing choices, fit configuration,
216	reference strategy, exclusions, and software version.
217	
218	Reference:
219	
220	Lin A. et al., "Minimum Reporting Standards for in vivo Magnetic Resonance
221	Spectroscopy (MRSinMRS): Experts' consensus recommendations."
222	DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/nbm.4484
223	
224	## Offline evidence boundary
225	
226	The task contains a code-oriented historical source snapshot, full project
227	manuals, method references, and deterministic scientific checkpoints. Large
228	scanner datasets, proprietary executables, GUI-only dependencies, and current
229	online project state are outside the offline execution path.
230	
231	The supplied evidence is intended to support investigation of the complete
232	scientific data flow rather than a single isolated function.

582	function rawWaterScaled = quantH2O(metsName, amplMets, amplWater, metsTR, waterTR, metsTE, waterTE,Bo)
583	
584	% Define constants
585	PureWaterConc       = 55500;            % mmol/L
586	WaterVisibility     = 0.65;             % assuming pure white matter
587	metsTE              = metsTE * 1e-3;
588	waterTE             = waterTE * 1e-3;
589	metsTR              = metsTR * 1e-3;
590	waterTR             = waterTR * 1e-3;
591	
592	% Look up relaxation times
593	
594	switch Bo
595	    case '3T'
596	        % 3T Water
597	        % From Wansapura et al. 1999 (JMRI)
598	        %        T1          T2
599	        % WM   832 +/- 10  79.2 +/- 0.6
600	        % GM  1331 +/- 13  110 +/- 2
601	        T1_Water            = 1.100;            % average of WM and GM, Wansapura et al. 1999 (JMRI)
602	        T2_Water            = 0.095;            % average of WM and GM, Wansapura et al. 1999 (JMRI)
603	
604	    case '7T'
605	        % 7T Water
606	        %        T1          T2
607	        % WM    1220         50
608	        % GM    2130         55
609	        T1_Water            = 1.675;            % average of WM and GM, Rooney et al. 2007 (MRM)
610	        T2_Water            = 0.0525;            % average of WM and GM, Bartha et al. 2002 (MRM)
611	end
612	
613	for mm = 1 : size(amplMets,1)
614	    % Metabolites
615	    for ss = 1 : size(amplMets,3)
616	        for kk = 1:length(metsName.metab{mm,ss})
617	            [T1_Metab_GM(kk), T1_Metab_WM(kk), T2_Metab_GM(kk), T2_Metab_WM(kk)] = lookUpRelaxTimes(metsName.metab{mm,ss},Bo);
618	            % average across GM and WM
619	            T1_Metab(kk) = mean([T1_Metab_GM(kk) T1_Metab_WM(kk)]);
620	            T2_Metab(kk) = mean([T2_Metab_GM(kk) T2_Metab_WM(kk)]);
621	            T1_Factor(kk) = (1-exp(-waterTR./T1_Water)) ./ (1-exp(-metsTR./T1_Metab(kk)));
622	            T2_Factor(kk) = exp(-waterTE./T2_Water) ./ exp(-metsTE./T2_Metab(kk));
623	
624	            % Calculate
625	            if ~isempty(amplMets{mm,1,ss})
626	                rawWaterScaled{mm,ss}.metab(kk,:) = (amplMets{mm,1,ss}.metab(kk,:) ./ amplWater) .* PureWaterConc ...
627	                    .* WaterVisibility .* T1_Factor(kk) .* T2_Factor(kk);
628	            end
629	        end
630	    end
631	end
632	end

655	function TissCorrWaterScaled = quantTiss(metsName, amplMets, amplWater, metsTR, waterTR, metsTE, waterTE, fGM, fWM, fCSF,Bo)
656	% This function calculates water-scaled, tissue-corrected metabolite
657	% estimates in molal units, according to Gasparovic et al, Magn Reson Med
658	% 55:1219-26 (2006).
659	
660	% Define Constants
661	switch Bo
662	    case '3T'
663	        % Water relaxation 3 T
664	        % From Lu et al. 2005 (JMRI)
665	        % CSF T1 = 3817 +/- 424msec - but state may underestimated and that 4300ms
666	        % is likely more accurate - but the reference is to an ISMRM 2001 abstract
667	        % MacKay (last author) 2006 ISMRM abstract has T1 CSF = 3300 ms
668	        % CSF T2 = 503.0 +/- 64.3 Piechnik MRM 2009; 61: 579
669	        % However, other values from Stanisz et al:
670	        % CPMG for T2, IR for T1
671	        % T2GM = 99 +/ 7, lit: 71+/- 10 (27)
672	        % T1GM = 1820 +/- 114, lit 1470 +/- 50 (29)
673	        % T2WM = 69 +/-3 lit 56 +/- 4 (27)
674	        % T1WM = 1084 +/- 45 lit 1110 +/- 45 (29)
675	        T1w_WM    = 0.832;
676	        T2w_WM    = 0.0792;
677	        T1w_GM    = 1.331;
678	        T2w_GM    = 0.110;
679	        T1w_CSF   = 3.817;
680	        T2w_CSF   = 0.503;
681	    case '7T'
682	        % Water relaxation 7 T
683	         % T1 from Rooney et al. 2007 (MRM)
684	         % T2 from Bartha et al. 2002 (MRM)
685	        T1w_WM    = 1.220;
686	        T2w_WM    = 0.050;
687	        T1w_GM    = 2.130;
688	        T2w_GM    = 0.055;
689	        T1w_CSF   = 4.425;
690	        T2w_CSF   = 0.141;
691	end
692	
693	% Determine concentration of water in GM, WM and CSF
694	% Gasparovic et al. 2006 (MRM) uses relative densities, ref to
695	% Ernst et al. 1993 (JMR)
696	% fGM = 0.78
697	% fWM = 0.65
698	% fCSF = 0.97
699	% such that
700	% concw_GM = 0.78 * 55.51 mol/kg = 43.30
701	% concw_WM = 0.65 * 55.51 mol/kg = 36.08
702	% concw_CSF = 0.97 * 55.51 mol/kg = 53.84
703	concW_GM    = 43.30*1e3;
704	concW_WM    = 36.08*1e3;
705	concW_CSF   = 53.84*1e3;
706	molal_concW = 55.51*1e3;
707	
708	% Gasparovic et al. method
709	% Calculate molal fractions from volume fractions (equivalent to eqs. 5-7 in Gasparovic et al., 2006)
710	molal_fGM  = (fGM*concW_GM) ./ (fGM*concW_GM + fWM*concW_WM + fCSF*concW_CSF);
711	molal_fWM  = (fWM*concW_WM) ./ (fGM*concW_GM + fWM*concW_WM + fCSF*concW_CSF);
712	molal_fCSF = (fCSF*concW_CSF) ./ (fGM*concW_GM + fWM*concW_WM + fCSF*concW_CSF);
713	
714	for mm = 1 : size(amplMets,1)
715	     for ss = 1 : size(amplMets,3)
716	        % Metabolites
717	        for kk = 1:length(metsName.metab{mm,ss})
718	            [T1_Metab_GM(kk), T1_Metab_WM(kk), T2_Metab_GM(kk), T2_Metab_WM(kk)] = lookUpRelaxTimes(metsName.metab{mm,ss}{kk},Bo);
719	            % average across GM and WM
720	            T1_Metab(kk) = mean([T1_Metab_GM(kk) T1_Metab_WM(kk)]);
721	            T2_Metab(kk) = mean([T2_Metab_GM(kk) T2_Metab_WM(kk)]);
722	
723	            % Calculate water-scaled, tissue-corrected molal concentration
724	            % estimates
725	            if ~isempty(amplMets{mm,1,ss})
726	                TissCorrWaterScaled{mm,ss}.metab(kk,:) = (amplMets{mm,ss}.metab(kk,:) ./ amplWater) .* molal_concW ...
727	                    .* (molal_fGM  * (1 - exp(-waterTR/T1w_GM)) * exp(-waterTE/T2w_GM) / ((1 - exp(-metsTR/T1_Metab(kk))) * exp(-metsTE/T2_Metab(kk))) + ...
728	                        molal_fWM  * (1 - exp(-waterTR/T1w_WM)) * exp(-waterTE/T2w_WM) / ((1 - exp(-metsTR/T1_Metab(kk))) * exp(-metsTE/T2_Metab(kk))) + ...
729	                        molal_fCSF * (1 - exp(-waterTR/T1w_CSF)) * exp(-waterTE/T2w_CSF) / ((1 - exp(-metsTR/T1_Metab(kk))) * exp(-metsTE/T2_Metab(kk)))) ./ ...
730	                        (1 - molal_fCSF);
731	            end
732	        end
733	     end
734	end
735	end
